title: the Sama Veda as song
hook: three singers sit down to talk shop, and one keeps asking: what holds that up? the answer goes all the way to space

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sama Veda as song, and the stobhas, the small sounds between the words that the Chandogya pairs with earth, wind and moon. Which small sound did you catch? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-eight.

Why is the sky blue? Because of the light. Why? Because of the air. Why? It's a game small children play at bedtime. Each answer gets its own why, and the questions only stop when someone runs out of answers, or patience. The Chandogya Upanishad tells a story that runs like that. Three men who are skilled in the high chant of the Sama Veda sit down together to talk about it. Two of them brahmins, one a king. And one question keeps getting asked, over and over, each time one step further down: what does that rest on? Today: what holds up a song.
screen: `WHY? BECAUSE. WHY?` → `THREE SINGERS SIT DOWN TOGETHER.` → `WHAT HOLDS UP A SONG?`

segments.voice: Their names are Shilaka, Dalbhya and Pravahana. Pravahana, the king, says: you two speak first, I'll listen. So Shilaka asks Dalbhya, in paraphrase: what does the saman, the chant, rest on? Dalbhya says: on tone, the sound of the voice. And tone? On breath. And breath? On food. And food? On water. And water? On that world, the heavens. And the heavens? Here Dalbhya stops. We don't lead the chant past the heavens, he says. We set it there. Shilaka isn't satisfied. He says the heavens rest on this world, the earth beneath us. Then the king speaks up, and Shilaka puts the question to him. And this world, what does it rest on? Pravahana's answer: on space. All beings come out of space and go back into space, he says. Space is greater than all of them. Space is the last support. And that, he says, is the high chant at its best: without end. Look at the shape of it. A song rests on a voice. The voice on breath. The breath on food. The food on water. And on down, until the floor underneath everything is open room. Not a thing, but the space things happen in. For a song, that's easy to hear. A note only rings because there's air and room around it. Sing into a pillow and it dies. In this story, the chant is grounded in what the king calls greater than all of them. And it took three people, patience, and one more question, to get there.
screen: `TWO BRAHMINS AND A KING.` · `TONE, BREATH, FOOD, WATER, HEAVEN.` · `AND THE EARTH? IT RESTS ON SPACE.` · `A NOTE RINGS BECAUSE THERE IS ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in the room between things. Sit, and notice the breath. At the end of each out-breath there's a small pause before the next breath comes. Let your attention rest in that pause, without stretching it. Then listen. Between one sound and the next, there's quiet. Rest there too. When a thought passes, notice the gap after it. Pause, quiet, gap: the open room everything else happens in. Let the breath come and go inside it. If you pray, you can rest in prayer there. The bell holds the time.
The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, three singers ask what the chant rests on: tone, breath, food, water, heaven, earth, and at last, space. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Sama Veda as song. Today, when you're sure you've reached the bottom of something, ask one more what does that rest on. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: The dialogue of Shilaka, Dalbhya and King Pravahana is taught from the Chandogya Upanishad, part of the Sama Veda's tradition, as a meditation on the high chant resting finally on space.

match.prompt: what the chant rests on — tap the pairs.
pairs: rests on space, says the king

myth: the three singers agree on the answer from the start
Dalbhya stops at the heavens, Shilaka goes to the earth, and the king goes on to space.
King Pravahana asks the other two to speak first
he says: you two speak first, I'll listen.
in the king's answer, all beings come out of space and go back into it
space is greater than all of them, the last support.

fork.setup: you're Dalbhya. the chain has reached the heavens. Shilaka asks: and what do the heavens rest on?
options: stop: we set the chant in the heavens
fork.reveal: Dalbhya stops there and won't lead the chant past the heavens. the conversation goes on without him: Shilaka names the earth, and the king names space.

original.note: Sanskrit: space, open room. In Chandogya 1.9 it is the last support of the high chant.

trapdoor: what you thought: a song rests on a good voice.
what it means: in the Chandogya, the chant rests on tone, breath, food, water, heaven, earth, and finally space.
what a scholar hears: gati, 'support' or 'goal', asked again and again until Pravahana answers ākāśa, from which all beings arise and into which they return (Chandogya 1.8–1.9).

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 1.8 (Shilaka, Dalbhya and Pravahana: the chant rests on tone, breath, food, water, the heavens, the earth)
Chandogya Upanishad 1.9.1–2 (all beings arise from space and return to it; space is the final support; the udgitha is without end)

notes: Names given in short form: Śilaka Śālāvatya, Caikitāyana Dālbhya, Pravāhaṇa Jaivali; confirm 'two priests and a king' (Pravāhaṇa as a kṣatriya king; the other two as brahmins).

Order of the chain (svara, prāṇa, anna, āpaḥ, 'that world', 'this world', ākāśa) and who says which step are given from memory; confirm. In the text Dālbhya stops at 'that world' and Śilaka names 'this world'.
'Without end' for the udgitha as parovarīyas / ananta in 1.9.2; confirm the paraphrase.
'Sing into a pillow and it dies' is an everyday illustration, not a claim about the text.

Editor pass: 'two priests' changed to 'two brahmins' (Pravahana's own word in 1.8); the final question is now put to the king by Shilaka, as in the text, rather than asked by the king himself; the practice was rewritten (rest in the pauses between breaths, sounds and thoughts) because the floor-ground-space body scan repeated 1262, 1265 and 1275.
